description: Hi! ​I'm Ashley. I study Communication for development. And My team aims to create the most optimized and innovative health monitoring software for astronauts.
summary:
YIRA (Your Integrated Responsive Assistant) is a physical and psychological health monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions to Mars. It compares each crew member’s indicators with their digital twin, a personal profile of health ranges calibrated before flight, including in partial gravity, and issues tiered alerts with a suggested action and protocol. It works entirely on board, because communication delays of up to 22 minutes and blackouts rule out real-time telemedicine.

We developed four integrated parts: a screenless wristband for continuous monitoring, with its electronics and a five-day battery life; a monitoring room with clinical equipment, housed in Orion-S, our conceptual redesign of the Artemis II Orion capsule; the YIRA software, with seven modules; and Yiri, a virtual assistant that guides sessions without inferring emotions or delivering diagnoses. The design draws on NASA data, the NASA-STD-3001 standard, and a physician interview, and our signal simulation with NeuroKit2 and NumPy demonstrates how alerts are triggered.

YIRA matters because on the way to Mars, astronauts must detect health changes themselves. It keeps working in layers: if the room fails, the wristband still alerts on its own.
details:
YIRA brings personalized monitoring, health-data analysis, medical guidance, and a supportive interface into one system for long-duration space missions. Our team developed a cross-platform software prototype, reproducible physiological simulations, and complementary hardware designs supported by 3D models, connection schematics, and power estimates.

The central idea is to compare each astronaut with their own health history. YIRA’s digital twin is a personalized, versioned profile containing baseline measurements, reference ranges, medical thresholds, and accumulated observations. Measurements are evaluated against both personal ranges and clinician-defined limits. This approach is intended to highlight gradual changes that could be overlooked when reviewing isolated readings.

The backend uses pandas for time-series processing and NumPy for statistical analysis, including median-based baselines, median absolute deviation, standardized deviations, and trend calculations. The functional design covers seven modules: crew overview, history and trends, alerts and actions, detailed assessments, medical protocols, baseline and threshold management, and reports for Earth. Alerts identify the affected indicator and connect it with a suggested response. Medical decisions remain under human supervision.

The proposed wristband collects physiological and activity data, while scheduled clinical sessions provide additional measurements and calibration. Its design includes heart-rate monitoring, oxygen-saturation measurements, skin temperature, movement, sleep estimates, and an on-demand single-lead ECG. Selected components include an nRF52840 microcontroller, MAX86141 optical front end, MAX30003 ECG front end, BMI270 motion sensor, local memory, and Bluetooth connectivity. A screen-free interface uses vibration and colored LEDs. The estimated power budget targets at least five days of operation; this remains a design estimate pending physical testing.

We also modeled a clinical monitoring room containing medical equipment, redundant computers, networking, charging stations, and backup power. Orion-S, our conceptual adaptation of the Orion capsule, provides a spatial framework for exploring that integration. It remains an engineering concept with unresolved launch-mass and reentry constraints. The room could be adapted to a larger transit vehicle or surface habitat.

Yiri gives the system a recognizable, approachable presence through an animated 3D character. Its expressions reflect the system’s health status. The broader design includes guided checkups, preventive reminders, symptom reporting, and voluntary questionnaires about mood and team well-being. Psychological information comes from explicit reports rather than inferred emotions. Informed consent, confidentiality, controlled access, and medical oversight shaped these requirements.

Communication delays influenced the architecture throughout. The mission concept places monitoring and decision support onboard, with reports queued for transmission when a connection becomes available. The proposed wristband retains local thresholds so it can continue alerting if the monitoring room becomes unavailable. In the current mobile implementation, Workbox caches the application interface and previously retrieved health data; complete autonomous operation requires deploying the backend onboard and validating the full system.

Our software uses Python, Django, Django REST Framework, django-allauth, and PostgreSQL. The shared interface uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui with Base UI. We use a Progressive Web App for mobile access, Bubblewrap for Android packaging, and Electron for desktop applications. Three.js renders Yiri. Docker Compose, Dev Containers, uv, and pnpm support a reproducible development environment.

For engineering and demonstration, we used Autodesk Fusion, Blender, CadQuery, trimesh, matplotlib, and Canva. NeuroKit2 and NumPy generate synthetic signals and repeatable scenarios that demonstrate changes in measurements and alert escalation. Public NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources, NASA-STD-3001, and a physician interview informed our requirements. Claude assisted with research synthesis, documentation, and selected code-generated engineering assets, which the team reviewed.

YIRA’s creative contribution is the integration of personalized baselines, physical and psychological monitoring, layered resilience, and a friendly interface within a spacecraft-aware design. We considered comfort, power, space, redundancy, privacy, measurement quality, and crew workload. The intended impact is to support earlier recognition of health changes and more informed onboard decisions. Physical sensor integration, aerospace-medical validation, and usability testing are the next steps.
